SOCIAL AND RELATIONSHIP CAPITAL
Health at the Centre of Our Outreach 
Health was where our community work reached the farthest in 
FY 2025-26, touching more than 4,52,000 lives. We treated the general public without charge through our General Hospital at Neyveli, and we strengthened public health institutions where they were most stretched. Our significant intervention addressed infant and maternal mortality in Cuddalore district. Working with the district administration and the Government Medical College Hospital, we provided advanced neonatal and obstetric equipment to the hospital and to government facilities across the district. The result was stronger emergency care for mothers and newborns, and a demonstration of what convergence between a public enterprise, a health department and a district administration can achieve for public health outcomes.
Learning that Opens Opportunity
Education cornered ₹10.01 crore of our investment and reached 39,834 students and young people, and we approached it as a continuum from a child's first years to a young adult's first job. We supported the running of 10 NLC schools and uplifted the quality of learning through smart boards, digital facilities and school sanitation, while investing in the fabric of education through classrooms, STEM laboratories, furniture and drinking water. 
We backed Jawahar Science College at Neyveli, worked to raise 
learning levels across 140 Anganwadi centres, and supported the Sneha Opportunity School for children with special needs. Our reach crossed states, with Integrated Science Centres for 1,800 students in Rajasthan and classroom furniture for 500 tribal students in Odisha.

Water security ran through much of our FY 2025-26 work, 
addressed from both ends: getting clean water to people, and replenishing the resource itself. We built potable water schemes in the Jharsuguda and Sambalpur districts of Odisha, restored the Manimuktha River, rejuvenated traditional tanks and ponds, and constructed check dams, overhead tanks and village water infrastructure. Together these improved access to safe water, recharged groundwater and supported the sustainable use of a scarce resource in regions where water shapes daily life.
The reach was measurable. The rejuvenation of minor-irrigation 
tanks in Cuddalore benefitted 22,318 people, and RO plants and drinking water infrastructure reached more than 2,200 rural residents in Ariyalur.

We treated sanitation as a matter of public health, not just 
infrastructure. Across our project areas we built sanitation assets and carried out Swachh Bharat activities, alongside rural infrastructure that improved the conditions of everyday life. Our environmental work in the community extended into afforestation and ecological care, so that our commitment to the environment reached beyond our own boundaries into the villages around us. This work sits alongside the operational stewardship described in our Natural Capital, two sides of a single responsibility.
Standing with the Communities We Affect
For the communities most directly touched by our mining, our responsibility runs deepest, and it defines what a just transition means in practice. We conduct land acquisition and rehabilitation in line with government policy and statutory frameworks, working with State Governments, District Administrations and Revenue Authorities to ensure fair compensation, resettlement support and the restoration of livelihoods for affected families.
What sets our approach apart is that it does not stop at statute. 
In consultation with local stakeholders, we build lasting community assets in mining-affected villages, school buildings, laboratories, water and sanitation infrastructure, healthcare and sports facilities and community amenities, and we keep an open grievance channel, engaging community representatives and authorities on questions of land, rehabilitation and implementation, and folding their feedback into how we plan. In this way, the regions that gave the nation its power continue to share in the progress that power created.
Delivering through Partnership
We work through a convergence model with the District Collectors and Administrations of Cuddalore, Ariyalur, Thanjavur, Virudhunagar, Bikaner, Jharsuguda and Sambalpur to identify needs and implement projects, and with government departments and agencies, from the District Rural Development Agency and the Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department to Municipal Corporations and the School Education, Health and Social Welfare Departments, so that our work converges with public programmes rather than duplicating them.
We deliver alongside educational institutions such as 
Annamalai University and government schools, and through capable implementation partners, including CHILDS Trust in Tamil Nadu, the Parichay Foundation in Odisha and the Global Happiness Foundation in Rajasthan. Local institutions, Panchayat Raj bodies, Village Development Committees and School Management Committees, take part in identifying, implementing and monitoring the work, which keeps it honest, accountable and rooted in genuine local priorities.We also drew a direct line from education to livelihood. With Annamalai University, we supported a Diploma in Mining Engineering for 180 students, opening a route from classroom to employment for rural youth, and we ran further skilling programmes through the University and the National Power Training Institute. Alongside these, our community programmes on the prevention of child marriage, on STEM learning and on extracurricular development widened opportunity for young people and women.

Renewable generation, an all-time highPerformance at a glance (FY 2025-26)Natural 
Capital
Natural Capital is both the resource base we depend on and the environment we are responsible for. 
As a lignite and coal-based generator, we manage our impact on air, water, land and biodiversity with care, and we are rebalancing our portfolio towards renewables and clean energy so that we can meet the nation's energy needs more sustainably. Responsible stewardship of natural resources runs through our mining, generation and diversification activities alike.Managing greenhouse gases
We recognise our responsibility to limit greenhouse gas 
emissions and align with the nation's climate goals. As a power generator relying significantly on lignite, we account for our emissions and work towards bringing down their intensity as our clean energy capacity grows, through efficiency improvements, clean technologies and disciplined investment in renewables.
Our Scope 1 emissions rose modestly in FY 2025-26, in 
step with higher generation across the group. Our Scope 2 emissions, by contrast, fell sharply to about an eighth of the previous year's level as we drew a far greater share of our auxiliary and administrative power from renewable sources. The direction of these two numbers captures our approach in miniature: The emissions is tied to the power that we generate move with demand, while the emissions within our own control continue to come down.
Reducing GHG gas emissions 
Our main lever for reducing greenhouse gas emissions is the steady expansion of our renewable portfolio, so that cleaner generation displaces a growing share of our fossil-based output over time. We are investing over ` 50,000 crore to scale our 
renewable capacity from around 1.43 GW to 10.11 GW by 2030, while our corporate target is to reach a 50% renewable share in our portfolio by 2030 and 77% by 2047, supporting India's goal of net-zero emissions by 2070. To give our renewable arm the room to grow with this momentum, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has approved a special exemption from the investment guidelines that apply to a Navratna company, enabling NLC India Renewables Limited to invest in green power projects free of the net-worth ceiling that would otherwise limit such investment.Carbon capture research
We are also pursuing carbon capture at source, the harder part of the emissions problem for a thermal generator. Our research collaboration with the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, established through a binding Memorandum of Understanding in May 2025 and fully funded by us, will be moving from a laboratory-scale study towards a pilot demonstration under Phase-II, and it reflects our intent to tackle carbon dioxide from combustion directly rather than through offsets alone.
Efforts towards energy management
Energy stewardship is an essential pillar of our sustainability strategy, underpinning both prudent use of national energy resources and the efficiency of our own operations. We pursue it through systematic replacement of conventional equipment with energy-efficient alternatives, regular maintenance, and upgrading our in-house expertise. These measures deliver tangible operational gains and build a culture of conservation across our mining and power operations.
Much of our conservation work in FY 2025-26 ran well ahead 
of the targets we set for it. We replaced 5,904 conventional light fittings with LED lamps, close to half as many again as our target for the year, and installed 134 automatic timers against a target of 40. We introduced 42 capacitor banks in the conveyor and equipment motors across our three mines to improve the power factor and cut reactive-power losses, replaced 327 ceiling fans with energy-efficient brushless DC motor fans, and extended dynamic loading systems across the conveyors of all three Neyveli mines. 
To reduce diesel use across surface transport, mining equipment 
and cranes, we implemented a fuel automation system using RFID technology. We also marked Energy Conservation Week in December 2025 with awareness drives that reached our employees and the public and, as a new step this year, a class for the children at our Neyveli boys' school.2,51,54,950

Green growth and decarbonisation
Advancing low-cost, low-carbon technologies of energy 
transition is central to how we plan our growth. We are laying out a decarbonisation roadmap across our operations and infrastructure, carried forward through capacity targets set out in our Corporate Plan 2030 and through our two dedicated green subsidiaries. This work aligns our expansion with India's wider transition to cleaner energy while strengthening the reliability of the power we supply.
Getting deeper into renewables
By diversifying our energy mix and reducing our carbon footprint, we continue to expand our renewable portfolio at pace, working towards the 10.11 GW target we have set for 2030. We are building this capacity both for our own account and in partnership. We are advancing solar and wind projects across states, including a 150 MW solar-wind hybrid project awarded by the Solar Energy Corporation of India, for which letters of award were issued to Ionx Wind Limited for a 100 MW solar project and to Enerture Technologies Private Limited for a 50 MW wind project. We have secured a 600 MW solar project at Khavda in Gujarat through a power purchase agreement with Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited, and won a 500 MW solar tender from the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency under the CPSU scheme, with development awarded to Tata Power Solar Systems Limited and Kosol Energie Private Limited. Through joint ventures, we are developing renewable projects at a larger scale still, including a 2,000 MW ultra-mega solar project under formation with TANGEDCO and a 5,000 MW solar programme through our joint venture with Coal India Limited.
Integrating green power into operations
We have drawn up a strategy with renewables claiming an increasing share of the energy that feeds our sites. We have installed captive solar plants across our townships and complexes, including rooftop solar on our non-residential buildings at Neyveli and a 200 kW floating solar array on the TPS-I lake, and a hybrid wind-solar system at our research centre. Small against the scale of the capacity we build for the grid, these installations reduce the carbon intensity of running our own operations and demonstrate the technologies we deploy at larger scale elsewhere.NATURAL CAPITAL
Research in green technologies
Our energy transition is supported by research into the technologies that will shape it. We have strengthened our collaborations with academic and research institutions, we are carrying forward pilot projects in green hydrogen and in our lignite-to-methanol pathway, and developing advanced carbon capture as part of the agreement with IIT Madras. 
Innovating energy storage
The supply of steady and reliable green power depends on storage. As part of our initiative to build storage capacity in our portfolio, we have rolled out our first large-scale battery energy storage system, a 250 MW/500 MWh project in Tamil Nadu awarded by TANGEDCO, secured through a purchase agreement with the Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited, for which the land agreement has been signed. This project allows us to store renewable generation and release it when the grid needs it most, enabling greater grid stability and the use of clean power we produce.Diversifying to tap into opportunities
Our energy management extends into new businesses built on our core strengths. Our lignite-to-methanol facility offers a route to higher-value products from the resources we mine, consistent with the direction of India's energy transition. We are also exploring opportunities in electric-vehicle infrastructure, where rising demand and supportive government policy create the prospect of charging stations and associated energy-storage facilities along national and state highways, drawing on our combined expertise in solar power generation and battery storage. These opportunities extend the value of our resource base and our capabilities into the business of a cleaner energy economy.

FY 2025FY 2026Air Emissions
Our operations chiefly generate particulate matter from excavation, drilling, haulage and storage. Oxides of sulphur and nitrogen 
and fly ash are produced from combustion in our thermal units. We acknowledge these impacts and address them through control at source, continuous monitoring and a robust framework of compliance.
Controlling and reducing emissions
In our mining areas, we suppress the dust produced by mining. An extensive water-spraying system covers haul roads, conveyors, working faces, vehicle movement and bunker areas, supported by the practice of wet drilling, so that dust is contained before it can travel. Our electrically operated bucket wheel excavators and belt conveyors, maintained over three decades, keep the carbon load and the emissions of our mining materially lower than that in diesel-based extractions. The three-tier green belts we develop around our bunker and mining areas trap dust while adding to the green cover of the region.In our thermal stations, we control emissions through the technology we have built into the plants. Electrostatic precipitators capture particulate matter, our supercritical boilers generate power more efficiently, and we are in the process of adopting flue gas desulphurisation to bring down sulphur emissions further. Our monitored sulphur dioxide readings remained above our desired levels, and the phased introduction of flue gas desulphurisation across our units is the response we are putting in place. We are also pursuing carbon capture at source through our 2025 pact with IIT Madras. The research collaboration is fully funded by us that moves from a laboratory study to a pilot demonstration, tackling carbon dioxide from combustion directly.NATURAL CAPITAL

(Kilo Litres)Water withdrawal  
(Kilo Litres)Water discharge (surface, greenbelt, 3rd party domestic) (Kilo Litres)Water recycled (greenbelt, irrigation, 3rd party domestic) (Kilo Litres)Water and Effluent Management
Our operations, particularly mining and thermal power 
generation, depend on a rigorous framework that ensures water is used efficiently, treated responsibly, and replenished wherever possible. By continuously improving how we handle water, we aim to protect the ecological balance and safeguard the needs of the communities around us.
Our water story begins with the geology of the field itself. The 
lignite we mine at Neyveli lies beneath a confined aquifer, which has to be de-pressurised through controlled pumping before mining can proceed safely. Rather than treat that pumped water as waste, we put it to use: the greater part feeds our thermal power stations, and the balance is sent to nearby villages for agricultural use, so that water raised for mining serves generation and farming before it returns to the land. Our total water withdrawal rose during the year, in step with the higher scale of our mining and generation, and the larger share of what we draw continues to be reused rather than discharged.
We manage the quality of our water as carefully as the quantity. To control the suspended solids that mining washes into water through seepage and surface run-off, we have constructed siltation wells and weirs along the canals in and around our mines. The wastewater from our operations, from station blowdown, vehicle washing and domestic use, passes through sewage and effluent treatment plants across our sites and townships, and the treated water is returned to use for gardening, greenbelt development, industrial washing and irrigation. Our water and wastewater are sampled and tested every month by the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board or accredited laboratories, and the results stay within permissible limits.
Beyond using water well, we work to return it to the ground. 
Across our office premises and larger buildings, rainwater harvesting structures channel run-off through check dams and percolation wells, and our monitoring shows the water table recharging as a result. In the recharge zone of the Neyveli groundwater basin, under the Government of India Coal Science and Technology scheme and with the technical assistance of IIT Madras, we have studied and built percolation ponds, recharge wells and check dams in the villages of Nadiyapattu and Maligampattu, and our continuous monitoring of piezometers has shown the percolation-pond technique to be the most effective for the Neyveli basin. 
To check the decline in the pressure surface of the deep confined 
aquifer, we have also taken up artificial recharge through injection wells, in a global collaboration with Rheinbraun Engineering of Germany and IIT Madras, tested at depths of around 250 metres in the complex aquifer conditions of the Neyveli region. We monitor the resource regionally through observation wells established in consultation with the Central Ground Water Board, and we prepare our water balance from continuous data on pumping, water levels and quality.
Ambient air quality monitoring
We monitor our air quality continuously and independently. The State Pollution Control Board conducts periodical surveys of ambient air quality in our mining units, and our own NABL-accredited laboratory at the Centre for Applied Research and Development monitors air quality on alternate days in line with our Consent to Operate. We have installed 13 ambient air quality stations in villages surrounding the industrial units. Ten of these are located in surrounding villages and monitored by a third-party NABL Accredited laboratory, the results are well within permissible limits and submitted to the statutory authorities. Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Systems are also installed at in and around our industrial units to monitor the Ambient Air Quality in real-time. During FY 2025-26, we recorded no incidents of environmental non-compliance.

Waste Management
We pursue waste management as an essential pillar of our 
sustainable operations, with a strong emphasis on resource efficiency, environmental responsibility and regulatory compliance. We treat waste not simply as something to be disposed of, but as a valuable resource, and this conviction runs through our Board-approved Waste Management Policy, prepared by our Corporate Environment Cell and applied across all our establishments. The policy follows a clear waste hierarchy, prevention first, then minimisation, reuse, recycle and recovery, with disposal as the last resort, and it holds our business unit heads responsible for implementation, requiring them to report the quantity of waste generated against the previous year at each quarterly Board meeting.

At the centre of our waste management is the principle we 
practise as waste into wealth: the idea that a material should be used to its fullest before it is ever treated as waste. This philosophy is guided by the 6R approach, refuse, rethink, reduce, repair, reuse and recycle, and it shapes how we handle the largest of our byproducts. Fly ash, the residue of burning lignite and coal, is managed scientifically and channelled to cement and brick manufacturers, so that a byproduct of our generation becomes an input for the construction industry. Our research teams extend the value we draw from fly ash further still, into rare earth elements, geopolymer building materials and high-purity silica, work carried in detail in our Intellectual Capital.Manufactured sand from overburden
A notable step in our circular-economy work is the conversion of mine overburden into manufactured sand. By processing the overburden from lignite mining into M-Sand, we offer a sustainable substitute for natural river sand, reducing the burden that sand mining places on riverine ecosystems while turning a mining byproduct into a material of value. This work reduces our reliance on natural resources and reinforces the framework of responsible resource management that our waste policy sets out.Biodiversity conservation
We hold the conviction that economic growth and ecological preservation must proceed hand-in-hand. Safeguarding biodiversity is fundamental to our operations and to the environmental legacy we leave behind, and we approach it through the systematic reclamation of mined land, extensive afforestation, and the conservation of the habitats around our operations.
Land reclamation
Mining is a temporary use of land. At the project formulation stage of every mine, we prepare a comprehensive plan to rehabilitate the land our operations disturb, so that the ground returns to productive use as mining moves on. We backfill the mined-out areas and reclaim them through three complementary methods: physical reclamation by land levelling, dozing and the conservation of topsoil; chemical reclamation using soil amendments and inorganic fertilisers; and biological reclamation using bio-fertilisers, green manure and green leaf manure. The reclaimed land is put to use for agriculture, horticulture, pasture and the development of green belt. Through more than six decades of what we practise as clean and green mining, this reclamation has created a substantial green cover in and around our mining areas.
Cultivation on reclaimed land
We have taken our reclamation a step further, turning mined-out land back to agriculture through collaborative projects under the Ministry of Coal's Science and Technology programme. Under our Hi-Tech cultivation project, run with Annamalai University and Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, we grow vegetables on the inert soils of our mined-out lands at three Neyveli mines using drip irrigation and mulching. In our polyhouses, in collaboration with IISc Bengaluru, we raise high-quality vegetables through hydroponics, an automated, soil-free method that grows produce through a water circulation system. These projects show that land once mined can be returned to agricultural value.Afforestation and green cover
We run afforestation programmes across our operations and raise saplings in our own polyhouses for planting. The three-tier green belts we develop around our bunker and mining areas trap dust, shelter wildlife and add to the green cover of the region. 
During the FY 2025-26, NLCIL has reclaimed over 133 Ha of 
the mined out land and biologically reclaimed about 126 Ha with over 1.3 lakh tree plantation.
Avifaunal diversity, eco-tourism and habitat creation
A dedicated avifaunal study in Neyveli highlighted the region’s richness in birdlife, documenting 107 species—77 terrestrial and 30 wetland varieties—across 59 families. While the majority (104 species) were classified as ‘Least Concern’ under the IUCN Red List (2016), three species were found to be ‘Near Threatened’, underscoring the importance of continued protective measures. This study provides a crucial baseline for future monitoring and conservation research, enabling NLCIL to adaptively manage habitats for avian species.
Mission LiFE
Mission LiFE, the Lifestyle for Environment initiative introduced by the Government of India at the 2021 United Nations climate summit, calls on individuals and communities to adopt sustainable lifestyles in harmony with nature. We have embraced its principles by weaving them into our operations and into our engagement with the communities around us, so that our environmental commitment reaches beyond our own boundaries into everyday behaviour.FY 2025

 NLC Talabira Thermal Power Project (3 X 800 MW)
 NLC Talabira Thermal Power Project (NTTPP), is a coal based thermal power project with an aggregate capacity 2400 MW, comprising three units of 800 MW capacity each. The project is proposed to be set up at Jharsuguda & Sambalpur District in the State of Odisha and will be linked to the allocated captive mine, Talabira Mines. The total estimated project cost is

Profit After Tax ( ₹ crore) 238.15 (49.90)Ash Management at NLCIL
Your Company continues to pursue environmentally responsible 
and sustainable management of fly ash and bottom ash generated 
from its Thermal Power Stations, with emphasis on maximising 
beneficial utilisation and ensuring environmentally sound disposal 
in compliance with the applicable MoEF&CC Fly Ash Notifications 
and guidelines issued by the Ministry of Power (MoP).
The Company continues to achieve 100% utilisation of fly 
ash generated from its Thermal Power Stations through 
environmentally sound and approved avenues, including its use in 
cement, bricks, blocks and other value-added products. Bottom ash 
is managed through scientifically controlled disposal and beneficial 
utilisation, including its deployment in infrastructure and road 
projects, in accordance with applicable MoEF&CC notifications 
and guidelines. Appropriate measures are undertaken for the safe 
handling, transportation, containment and monitoring of ash to 
minimise potential environmental impacts.
As part of its continued efforts towards resource recovery and advancing circular economy principles, the Company is 
progressively promoting value addition and reducing dependence 
on ash disposal facilities. In a significant step towards this objective, 
the Company entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) 
with BARC on 06 August, 2025 for the extraction of Rare Earth 
Elements (REEs) from fly ash. A pilot plant is proposed to be 
established at Neyveli and is targeted to be operational by the end of 2027. This initiative is expected to support sustainable resource 
utilisation and contribute to the nation’s critical mineral objectives.
Through these initiatives, the Company remains committed to responsible ash management, regulatory compliance, 
environmental protection and resource efficiency. The Company 
will continue to explore and implement innovative pathways for the 
beneficial utilisation, resource recovery and value creation from fly 
ash and bottom ash, in furtherance of its sustainability and circular 
economy objectives.

DIRECTORS’ REPORT (CONTD.)Coal Linkage & Fuel Supply
The coal requirement for GTPP is linked to the Pachwara South OCP.
Mine development activities commenced in December 2025 and 
coal production commenced in March 2026.
The captive coal production is being ramped up progressively, with 
the rated capacity of 9 MTPA envisaged to be achieved in the fifth 
year of operation as per the approved mining plan.
Until the required level of captive coal production is achieved, GTPP Project continues to meet its coal requirement through 
bridge linkage coal from Coal India Limited (CIL) mines as per 
the recommendations of the Standing Linkage Committee (Long 
Term) [SLC(LT)].
Accordingly, SLC(LT), vide its recommendation dated 30.03.2026, 
approved 6.58 Million Tonnes of bridge linkage coal from CIL mines 
for FY 2026-27 on a tapering basis. Based on the recommendation, CIL has allocated coal from:
• Eastern Coalfields Limited (ECL) – 2.990 MT
• Northern Coalfields Limited (NCL) – 1.113 MT
• Central Coalfields Limited (CCL) – 1.074 MT
Furthermore, in order to meet out the operational coal requirements 
of GTPP, NUPPL has also signed an MoU for 2 MT with NLCIL’s 
Talabira-II & III OCP Mines for FY 2026-27 and coal dispatch has started from 24.07.2026.
Project Progress & Expenditure
• The Project (GTPP & South Pachwara) achieved a Capital 
Expenditure (CAPEX) of ₹2,424.64 crore during FY 2025-26 
against the annual target of ₹1,500 crore, achieving 161.64% 
of the target.

Sustainability Development Measures
Scientific reclamation of mined-out land continued to remain 
one of the Company's flagship sustainability initiatives. During 
FY 2025-26, your Company successfully reclaimed more than 
126 hectares of mined-out land through scientific bio-reclamation 
and ecological restoration techniques. With this achievement, the 
cumulative  biologically reclaimed area has exceeded 2,900 hectares 
since inception, representing one of the largest mine reclamation 
programmes undertaken by any mining company in the country.The reclaimed areas have been transformed into ecologically sustainable landscapes comprising dense plantations, forests, eco-parks, grasslands, wetlands, water bodies and habitats 
supporting diverse flora and fauna. These reclamation efforts have 
substantially contributed towards restoration of degraded land, 
enhancement of biodiversity, carbon sequestration, improvement of 
soil quality, prevention of erosion and strengthening of the regional 
ecological balance.
During the year, Your Company continued large-scale afforestation 
and plantation programmes under Mission GREEN through active 
participation of employees, schools, local communities and other 
stakeholders during World Environment Day, Van Mahotsav and 
other environmental awareness campaigns. These initiatives have 
strengthened environmental consciousness while contributing to enhancement of the green cover across the Company's 
operational areas.
Your Company also continued scientific ecological monitoring 
of reclaimed mine areas through reputed academic and research 
institutions for assessment of vegetation growth, biodiversity, 
biomass accumulation and ecosystem sustainability. These studies 
provide valuable inputs for continuous improvement in reclamation 
practices and long-term environmental planning.
In line with its commitment to sustainable land utilisation, Your 
Company continued initiatives for repurposing mined-out lands 
for renewable energy projects, water resource development, sustainable, apiculture, pisciculture and other productive post-
mining land uses, thereby creating long-term environmental and 
socio-economic value.
Environmental Compliance and Resource 
Management
Your Company remains committed to maintaining the highest 
standards of environmental compliance across all mining, 
power generation and allied operations. A robust Environmental 
Management System (EMS) is implemented across all units to ensure compliance with statutory requirements and continual 
improvement in environmental performance.
During FY 2025-26, comprehensive environmental monitoring covering ambient air quality, stack emissions, water quality, 
noise levels and other environmental parameters was carried out 
through approved laboratories and continuous online monitoring 
systems. The monitored parameters remained within the 
prescribed regulatory standards, demonstrating the effectiveness 
of the Company's environmental management practices. As part 
of its continuous efforts to minimise environmental impacts, the 
Company further strengthened dust mitigation measures through 
extensive deployment of water sprinklers, fixed and mobile mist cannons, high-pressure spray systems, mechanised road cleaning 
equipment and other advanced dust suppression technologies across 
mines, transportation corridors and material handling facilities.
The Company continued to promote water conservation through 
efficient water management practices, recycling and reuse of 
treated wastewater, optimisation of freshwater consumption and 
strengthening of wastewater treatment infrastructure across its 
operational facilities.
During the year, Your Company successfully obtained Consent 
to Operate (CTO) from the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board 
for the Water Treatment Plant, Modern Sewage Treatment Plant and Airport facilities, further reinforcing its commitment to statutory compliance and environmentally responsible 
infrastructure management.
In compliance with the provisions of the Environment (Protection) 
Act, 1986 and subsequent amendments relating to emission 
standards for thermal power plants, the Company continued 
implementation of various emission reduction measures, including 
Flue Gas Desulphurisation (FGD) systems and other pollution control technologies, in accordance with applicable regulatory 
requirements and implementation schedules.

DIRECTORS’ REPORT (CONTD.)LAND ACQUISITION AND REHABILITATION & RE-SETTLEMENT
Land Acquisition and R&R Policy
Your Company is committed to minimising the socio-economic 
impact of land acquisition and displacement on Project Affected 
Persons (PAPs) through appropriate Rehabilitation & Resettlement 
(R&R) measures. Your Company implements R&R measures 
in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, 
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (RFCTLARR Act), the 
rules and notifications issued thereunder, and the R&R policies, 
rules, Government Orders and guidelines of the respective State 
Governments, as applicable to the projects.
The R&R measures adopted by Your Company are, wherever applicable, in addition to and over and above the statutory entitlements prescribed under the applicable Central and State laws, policies and Government orders. The Company also provides additional rehabilitation, resettlement, livelihood and 
developmental measures based on the specific requirements of the projects and the applicable approved R&R framework.
Apart from development of Resettlement Centres (RCs) in the vicinity of projects, Your Company provides essential 
infrastructure and civic amenities at these centres to facilitate the 
smooth resettlement of eligible Project Affected Families (PAFs). 
Rehabilitation measures are supplemented by payment of statutory 
compensation and, wherever applicable, enhanced compensation/
ex-gratia over and above statutory entitlements, with the support 
and coordination of the respective District Administrations.
A Grievance Redressal Mechanism is in place for addressing the 
grievances and representations of PAPs. Further, Your Company 
provides enhanced land compensation, wherever applicable, based on the prevailing Government Orders and approved 
R&R provisions, including payment of ex-gratia and settlement 
through Lok Adalats, based on applications received from eligible landowners who have handed over their lands and houses.Your Company also supports capacity building and skill 
development of PAPs. One-year Post-Graduate programmes are 
provided to eligible PAPs possessing Engineering and Diploma qualifications through the National Power Training Institute 
(NPTI). Training is also provided to PAPs selected as SME Operator 
Assistant Trainees and Mines Support Service Trainees under the 
three-year training programme, thereby facilitating sustainable 
employment and livelihood opportunities.
Your Company has put in place a structured mechanism for 
providing monthly annuity to eligible Project Affected Families 
(PAFs) through an insurance company. In the first phase, PAFs 
relating to the acquired and possessed land have been mapped with 
the insurance company, with the remaining eligible PAFs to be 
covered in subsequent phases.
Research and Development (R & D)
The Centre for Applied Research & Development (CARD) continues 
to serve as the in-house R&D Centre of your Company and has 
been recognised by the Department of Science & Technology since 
1975. CARD is accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) in accordance with the international standard ISO/IEC 17025:2017.
During the year under review, the NABL accreditation of CARD 
laboratories was renewed for the disciplines of Mechanical, Chemical and Biological Testing on 23.01.2026, valid up to 
22.01.2030. Further, the recognition of your Company's In-House 
R&D Unit was also renewed by the Department of Scientific and 
Industrial Research (DSIR), Ministry of Science & Technology, on 
09.03.2026, valid up to 31.03.2029.
Further, during FY 2025-26, the following two patent applications 
were filed:
• "A System and Method for IoT-Enabled Nutrient Dosing and 
Environmental Monitoring in Vertical Farming"
• "Environmentally Sustainable and Eco-Friendly Geo Polymer 
Brick Composition and Method of Manufacturing Utilising Fly 
Ash, M-Sand and GGBFS"
CARD functions as a multidisciplinary research and technical support unit, contributing to innovation, operational efficiency, 
and sustainability across the Company’s core sectors.
The major functions of CARD include:
• Undertaking Science & Technology (S&T) research projects 
aligned with the Company’s strategic objectives.
• Conducting environmental monitoring, pollution assessment, 
quality control testing, consultancy, and technical services.
• Promoting technology development, patenting, and commercialisation based on R&D outcomes and pilot plant 
studies, as well as coordinating S&T projects undertaken across 
the Company.
• Providing institutional support to students, carrying out special 
studies for operational improvement, and supporting new 
initiatives and schemes.
• Delivering analytical and testing services for quality assurance 
of materials used in mining, power generation, and other service units, including services to external agencies on a 
chargeable basis.
• Undertaking research in key areas such as lignite utilisation, 
product diversification, by-product utilisation, solid waste management, wasteland reclamation, renewable energy, clean coal technologies, and implementation of real-time 
monitoring systems.
The total expenditure incurred on Research & Development during 
the year 2025-26 is ₹44.53 crore .

Medical Facilities
Your Company has established a robust health care model for 
protecting, preserving and promoting the health and well-being of 
its workforce and the community. The model is time-tested with 
proven results, founded on the belief that a healthy workforce is 
the key driver of economic and organisational sustainability. Since 
the establishment of the NLC India Hospital (NLCIH) in 1962, 
your Company has continued to support and expand comprehensive 
medical services. NLCIL Hospital – a secondary level medical 
facility with a bed capacity of 350, catering not only to employees 
and their families but also to residents of peripheral villages. As 
part of fulfilling the social agenda of providing quality primary 
health care to external stakeholders, NLCIL hospital is treating 
rural patients free of cost in all its specialty departments on OP 
basis. By providing free access to quality medical care, NLCIL 
contributes to sustaining the livelihood of rural people as they need 
not have to spend on health care needs. An average of 1,000 patients 
are visiting every day in NLC India Hospital totalling to 3,65,000 patients a year. The facilities includes:
• 
Out-Patient Department (OPD) Services: The Hospital’s 
OPD services, supported by well-equipped diagnostic 
facilities, pharmacy and therapy services, catered to 3,65,449 
patients  during the year. Treatment was provided across 
various specialties, including General Medicine, General 
Surgery, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Paediatrics, Dermatology, 
Orthopaedics, Ophthalmology, ENT, Chest Medicine, 
Psychiatry, Dental and Ayurveda.
• In-Patient (IP) Services:  In-patient services were provided in 
General Medicine, General Surgery, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, 
Paediatrics, Orthopaedics, Ophthalmology and ENT, benefiting 
7,362 patients during the financial year.
• Laboratory and Blood Bank Services: Laboratory services 
remained an integral part of patient care, with more than 18 
lakh in-house laboratory investigations  conducted during the 
year. Blood donation initiatives were also undertaken to meet 
emergency healthcare requirements.
• Radiology Services:  Radiology services were strengthened 
through the upgradation of the Computed Radiography 
(CR) workstation. Nearly 600 X-rays were conducted for age 
assessment and around 6,000 chest X-rays were undertaken as part of Tuberculosis screening programmes.
• 
Emergency and Casualty Services: Round-the-clock Emergency and Casualty Services provided treatment to 47,416 patients during the year. Emergency transportation was supported by three Advanced Life Support (ALS) 
ambulances, one Basic Life Support (BLS) ambulance and 
15 empanelled ambulances , ensuring timely referral and 
emergency response.• Industrial Medical Centre (IMC): The IMC continued to 
play an important role in safeguarding occupational health by 
conducting statutory medical examinations.
• Occupational Hearing Health: Workers engaged in hazardous 
mining locations were subjected to audiometry  for the early 
detection of Noise-Induced Hearing Loss. Positive cases were 
followed up and rehabilitated through the ENT Department of 
the Hospital.
• Respiratory Health Screening: All workers were subjected 
to Lung Function Tests  for the early detection of respiratory 
problems. Positive cases were treated and followed up through the Chest Clinic of the Hospital.
• 
First Aid Training: First Aid training was initiated for 
Contract Indcoserve workers and SME IT personnel , with 
the approval of the competent authority. Around 156 persons 
were successfully trained during FY 2025-26 .
• Ayurveda Services:  Ayurveda services continued to gain 
wider acceptance, with 24,264 OP consultations  and 2,329 
Panchakarma therapy procedures conducted during the year.
• Yoga Services:  Six new Yoga batches , involving nearly  
300 participants , were introduced during the year. Yoga therapy 
services were also provided to 38 new patients .
• Ayurveda Day Care Facility: A Day Care treatment facility 
was introduced at the Ayurveda Dispensary, Block-8, and was 
utilised by 72 patients  during the year.
• Physiotherapy Services:  More than 11,000 physiotherapy 
sessions  were provided during the year. To strengthen 
rehabilitation services,  Class-IV Laser Therapy equipment 
was procured, installed and commissione d.
• Tertiary and Quaternary Care: 24 hospitals were empanelled 
for providing tertiary/quaternary care services to employees 
and beneficiaries.

DIRECTORS’ REPORT (CONTD.)Safety
Your Company remains committed to strengthening industrial 
safety  through proactive and innovative initiatives, continuous 
improvement in safety practices, and strict compliance with 
statutory requirements across all its Mines and Thermal 
Power Plants. 
Key measures undertaken to ensure safety of personnel and 
equipment include:
i.  The Company promotes blast-free mining practices across its 
mining operations, using advanced equipment such as Bucket 
Wheel Excavators, belt conveyors, spreaders, and surface 
miners, as well as conventional mining equipment, to enhance 
safety and reduce the risks associated with blasting.
ii.  All HEMM and Specialised Mining Equipment (SME) 
deployed in the Mines and Thermal Plants has been fitted with 
AFDSS (Automatic Fire Detection and Suppression System) and all other safety devices as per statutory guidelines.
iii.  Adequate Sufficient Fire Extinguishers are provided at have 
been provided at strategic locations across in workshops, 
offices, SME, Conveyor Drive heads and other critical area, 
with regular inspection and maintenance to ensure readiness., 
etc. and regularly checked and updated.
iv.  Annual safety audits of all Mines are conducted by a multi-
disciplinary Corporate Safety Team, while Thermal Power 
Plants undergo safety audits by accredited external agencies once in every two years.
v.  A new Corporate Safety Council Team, comprising  formed consisting of Executives and Workmen from Different Units has been constituted to conduct  ofmonthly safety inspection of designated units and present its findings to the  NLCIL to make inspection of the pre-determined unit every month and present its findings to the respective Unit head for necessary correction. and his team.
vi.  Regular safety Conducting workshops & Training 
programmes are conducted across Mines and Thermal Power 
Units through established on Safety in Mines and Thermal 
units in every Unit Training centre, well established Group 
VTC, Power station Training Centre and L&DC.
vii.  Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) have been established 
for all the activities of the mines and thermal plants and are 
strictly adhered to, ensuring safe, consistent, and standardised 
operations implemented.
viii.  Risk-based Safety Management Plans (SMPs) have been 
prepared and implemented for all major mining activities in 
accordance with the Coal Mines Regulations, 2017
ix.  Monthly safety committee meetings are conducted across all 
Mines and Thermal Power Plants, along with zonal, fire safety, 
and OEM safety meetings to review safety performance and address identified risks.
x.  Weekly Safety inspections of Mines, Thermal plants and REPP units are being carried out by Corporate Safety 
Executives and inspection report is submitted to concerned 
Units for compliance and improvement in safety standard.xi.  The Company Industrial Medical Centre serves as a recognised 
First Aid Training Centre, conducting regular training for 
workmen in accordance with DGMS, DGFASLI and DISH/
CIF requirements, with batches trained every month.
xii.  NLCIL Industrial Medical Centre has been recognised as 
training centre for imparting First Aid Training that meets 
the requirements of the DGMS initiatives and also the 
requirements of the industries under the DGFASLI, DISH/CIF 
and batches of workmen are trained on first aid every month.

Risk Management
The Company operates under a robust, Board-sanctioned Integrated 
Risk Management Policy and Framework. In addition to setting 
clear criteria for prioritising enterprise risks, it explicitly defines 
the roles and accountabilities of all key personnel. In line with 
policy guidelines, a sub-board Internal Risk Review Committee 
evaluates risk exposures every quarter, while the overarching risk assessment and mitigation protocols are regularly examined by the 
Risk Management Committee, Audit Committee, and the Board 
of Directors.
To manage exposure on foreign currency borrowings, NLCIL 
maintains a dedicated Foreign Exchange Risk Management Policy 
(FERMP). This framework balances the minimisation of debt 
servicing costs against exchange rate and interest rate fluctuations, fully aligned with the organisation's risk tolerance.
The primary aim of the FERMP is to continuously recognise, 
measure, and track foreign exchange and interest rate sensitivities. 
It utilises selective hedging mechanisms to control risks within acceptable boundaries while ensuring strict adherence to 
governance standards. By placing stability and risk containment 
above speculative profit, the policy protects NLCIL's long-term 
financial health.
Vigilance
Your Company has a robust Vigilance Department headed by the 
Chief Vigilance Officer (CVO), at the level of Joint Secretary to the Government of India, who advises the CMD on vigilance matters and coordinates with the CVC and CBI.
The Department continues to promote integrity, transparency, and 
accountability through a proactive and preventive approach, with 
focus on strengthening internal controls, transparent procurement, 
and ethical project and operational practices.
During FY 2025-26, preventive vigilance initiatives were 
strengthened across the Corporate Office and major project locations. The Department identified systemic vulnerabilities and implemented Systemic Improvement Measures (SIMs) to 
strengthen controls and mitigate operational and financial risks.
The Vigilance Department has evolved into a proactive governance 
partner, supporting risk mitigation and operational excellence 
through preventive vigilance, digital initiatives, ethical awareness, 
and systemic improvements, while upholding the highest standards 
of integrity, transparency, fairness, and accountability.

Centralised Payment Process of Stores and Spares
In your Company, the respective unit account centre except for 
the materials purchased by Permanent Central Stores (PCS) and 
Mines Sub Stores (MSS) carried out payment for spares and other 
materials purchased by units. For PCS and MSS, accounts centres of 
Material Management Complex (MMC) and Mine I carried out the 
payment, respectively. Thus, the centralised payment implemented 
in March, 2024 has helped in controlling the payments and reducing 
the time taken for making the payments.

2005

multiple financiers, thereby enhancing their liquidity. The Company 
remains committed to supporting MSMEs by ensuring prompt

Enterprises (DPE) directives.

discounting and improved liquidity.

  The executive summary of Impact Assessment of CSR 
Projects carried out in pursuance of sub-rule (3) of rule 8 is 
provided below:
  Introduction:  As part of its Corporate Social Responsibility 
(CSR) initiatives, NLCIL has undertaken wide range of social 
and developmental programmes in its operational areas and 
beyond, with a focus on community upliftment and fostering 
sustainable and inclusive growth.  During the FY 2023-24, the NLCIL has spent ₹47.36 crore 
CSR domains such as education, healthcare, drinking water, 
sanitation, water augmentation, skill development, rural sports, 
women's empowerment, and environmental sustainability 
among others. To evaluate the effectiveness and impact of these 
initiatives, IPE was entrusted to conduct impact assessment of 
11 CSR projects. These projects have been completed for not 
less than one year to assess their effectiveness in addressing 
the developmental needs of communities within and beyond 
NLCIL's operational areas. The study majorly focused on 
measuring outcomes, concentrating on the transformations 
experienced by target communities, including socio-economic 
improvements and enhanced livelihood opportunities. 
NLCIL's commitment to sustainability in its CSR initiatives 
guaranteed a lasting transformative impact, facilitated by 
the active involvement of local stakeholders. This approach 
reinforced NLCIL’s dedication in promoting meaningful 
change, transparency, and accountability in its CSR activities. 
Through these impact evaluations, NLCIL gained valuable 
insights into the achievements and outcomes of each project, 
further strengthening its commitment to fostering a positive 
societal impact.

A. Conservation of Energy
i.  The Active steps taken on Conservation of Energy 
during 2025-2026 and the impacts:
 1.  Energy Conservation is being achieved through regular 
maintenance, replacement of conventional equipment 
using energy efficient equipment and through innovative 
ideas using in-house expertise.
 2.  Multifarious methods were adopted to inculcate 
and imbibe the energy conservation measures in the industrial, Service units and in Administrative 
building also.
 3.  During this financial year more than 15 training programmes were organised in observance with promotion of fuel and energy conservation and one 
meeting was conducted towards EC measures.
 4.  The conventional lights are being replaced with 
contemporary energy saving LED lights. During this 
financial year 5904 Nos of conventional lights were 
replaced with LED lights which is 140.47% against the Target (4200) for 2025-2026.
 5.  134 Nos. Auto timers were installed which is 335% 
against target (40 Nos.)
 6.  Capacitor banks are being introduced in phased manner 
in motors of conveyors in all the three mines Special 
mining equipment and transformers to improve power 
factor thereby reducing reactive power energy losses. 
During this financial year 42 Nos. capacitor banks are 
installed which is 87.5% against target (48 Nos.)
 7.  Dynamic loading systems are installed in all the 
three Mines.
  a.  Installed in 2 conveyors of Mine-IA achieving 
100% of the target of 2 Nos.
  b.  inMine-1 materials were received and installed in three conveyors.
  c.  Already DLC is working in Lignite system of 
Mine-ll.
 8.  327 Nos of conventional ceiling fans were replaced with 
energy efficient Bush Less DC Motor (BLDC) Fans.
 9.  Two Number Solar water heaters were erected in General 
Hospital and Guest House.
 10.  Measures taken to reduce the consumption of diesel in 
various sectors (surface transport, mining equipment, 
cranes etc.) by implementing Fuel Automation system 
by installing RFID technology.
 11.   During this financial year the E-Vehicles procurement is Nil. 12.  In TS-II, 9 Nos. of battery operated tricycles for canteen 
were procured.
 13.  Energy conservation week was conducted during 14.12.2025-20.12.2025. During this period wide 
publicity and awareness was made by issuing flyers to all 
employees. Flyers were issued to the public in Arch gate, 
Main Bazar to create awareness. As a new initiative, an awareness class was conducted in NLCIL Boys School 
to emphasize the importance of Energy Conservation 
among school children. Energy conservation banners 
were placed in vital and common places – Arch gate, 
CBS, Main bazaar, Schools, etc to create awareness 
towards energy conservation.

B. Technology Absorption
  In pursuit of organisational excellence, industrial advancement and societal benefit, the Company continues 
to strengthen its research and innovation ecosystem through 
focused technology absorption initiatives. The Centre for 
Applied Research & Development (CARD) plays a pivotal 
role by collaborating with premier academic and research institutions to develop indigenous technologies, improve 
operational efficiency, and support sustainability initiatives.
(i) Efforts Made Towards Technology Absorption
1. Green Hydrogen:
  As part of its commitment to clean energy transition and 
decarbonisation, NLCIL has initiated the establishment of 
a 4 MW Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) electrolyser-based Green Hydrogen Plant at Neyveli, Tamil Nadu. The 
comprehensive Engineering, Procurement and Construction 
(EPC) contract was awarded to M/s. InSolare Energy Limited on 03.11.2025. The project is currently under 
implementation and is expected to contribute significantly 
towards the Company’s renewable energy portfolio and green 
hydrogen initiatives.
2.  Optimisation studies for patent ﬁling regarding 
application of humic acid for semiconductor 
applications
  CARD, NLCIL has undertaken a collaborative R&D project 
with IIT Madras on “Optimisation studies for patent filing 
regarding application of humic acid for semiconductor 
applications” through Joint Development Agreement entered 
on 21.10.2025. The project focuses on exploring the potential of lignite-derived humic acid as an environmentally friendly 
and cost-effective material for optoelectronic applications, 
particularly light-emitting devices. The ongoing study aims 
to optimise thin-film formation and tailor optical emission 
properties in the visible spectrum (blue, green, and red) to 
enable patentable innovations. This initiative is expected to 
open new avenues for value-added utilisation of lignite and 
contribute towards sustainable semiconductor technologies.
3.  Setting up a Pilot Scale Demonstration Facility 
for Recovery of Rare Earth Elements (REEs) from Lignite Coal Fly Ash
  NLCIL has entered Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) 
with Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) on 06.08.2025 
for “Setting up a Pilot Scale Demonstration Facility for 
Recovery of Rare Earth Elements (REEs) from Lignite Coal 
Fly Ash” at Neyveli. The project focuses on establishing a 
NLC India Limited

pilot-scale facility to demonstrate an innovative process 
for extraction of REEs from lignite fly ash, transforming an industrial by-product into a valuable source of critical 
materials. Rare earth elements are strategic resources with 
applications in clean energy technologies, electronics, 
healthcare, advanced manufacturing and national security. 
Under this collaboration, BARC provides technological and R&D support including process design, engineering and operational guidance, while NLCIL is responsible for infrastructure creation, plant execution, operation and 
maintenance. This initiative is expected to enable sustainable 
fly ash management, promote indigenisation of critical materials and strengthen the Company’s role in emerging 
high-technology sectors.
4.  Pilot Project for Production of Biohydrogen using 
Biomass
  CARD, NLCIL has undertaken a collaborative R&D project 
with Alagappa University, Karaikudi on “Pilot Project for 
Production of Biohydrogen using Biomass”. The project focuses on developing sustainable hydrogen production 
through anaerobic fermentation of biomass and wastewater 
using microbial processes. The study aims to optimise 
biohydrogen generation systems and integrate carbon capture 
techniques to minimise emissions. This initiative is expected 
to support clean energy transition and promote alternative 
hydrogen production pathways. The project is ongoing, with 
preliminary activities including process planning and system 
development under progress.
5.  Study on Effect of Lignite-Derived Humic Acid on 
Microbial Diseases in Aquaculture Systems
  A collaborative R&D initiative has been taken up by CARD, 
NLCIL with Annamalai University, Chidambaram on “Study on 
effect of lignite-derived humic acid (HA) on microbial diseases 
of intensive brackish water aquaculture systems”. The project 
focuses on evaluating lignite-derived humic acid as a feed additive 
to improve fish health and reduce microbial infections. The study 
aims to enhance growth performance and develop commercially 
viable applications. This initiative is expected to expand value-
added utilisation of lignite derivatives in aquaculture. The 
project is ongoing, with agreement formalisation completed and 
preparatory research activities initiated.
6.  Studies on Lignite Humic Acid and Its Value-Added 
Products for Agricultural Applications
  An R&D collaboration has been established between CARD, 
NLCIL and Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Coimbatore 
on “Studies on Lignite Humic Acid and its Value-Added 
Products for Application in Important Crops of Tamil Nadu”. 
The project focuses on assessing humic acid as a bio-stimulant 
for improving crop yield and soil health across different agro-
climatic regions. The study also aims to develop value-added 
formulations for agricultural use. This initiative is expected 
to promote sustainable agriculture practices. The project 
is ongoing, with field trials commenced across multiple 
locations using supplied samples.7.  Development of New Material for Bucket Wheel 
Excavator Teeth and Life Enhancement
  A joint R&D project has been undertaken by CARD, NLCIL 
with National Institute of Technology, Tiruchirappalli (NITT) 
on “Development of new material for bucket wheel teeth and 
its life improvement”. The project focuses on developing 
advanced materials and improved designs to enhance wear 
resistance and durability of excavator components. The study 
aims to reduce downtime and improve mining efficiency. 
The project is ongoing, with material characterisation and 
laboratory testing activities in progress.
8.  Materials and Process Design for Alternative to 
Tungsten Carbide Bucket Teeth Inserts
  CARD, NLCIL in collaboration with Indian Institute of 
Science, Bangalore (IISc) is executing an R&D project on 
“Materials and Process Design for Alternative to Tungsten 
Carbide Excavator Bucket Teeth Inserts for Mining Industry”. 
The project focuses on developing cost-effective and high-
performance alternative materials for mining applications. 
The study aims to improve durability and reduce reliance on expensive materials.
  The project is ongoing, with alloy design completed and 
further material development and validation in progress.
9.  Bene ﬁciation of Silica Sand for Solar-Grade 
Applications
  A collaborative R&D effort between CARD, NLCIL and Council of Scientific and Industrial Research - Institute of Minerals and Materials Technology (CSIR-IMMT), 
Bhubaneswar is underway on “Beneficiation studies for the 
production of high pure silica from silica sand for solar glass/
panel/wafer manufacturing applications”. The project focuses 
on developing processes to upgrade silica purity suitable for 
solar applications. The study aims to reduce impurities and 
enable indigenous sourcing for solar industries. The project is 
ongoing, with beneficiation studies progressing and improved 
silica purity achieved at laboratory scale.
10.  Development of Metal Supported Solid Oxide Fuel 
Cells (MS-SOFCs) using Lignite Fly Ash
  CARD, NLCIL has initiated a collaborative R&D project with 
Annamalai University, Chidambaram on “Development of 
Indigenous Technology to Manufacture Metal Supported 
Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (MS-SOFCs) using the Materials derived from Lignite Fly Ash by Atmospheric Plasma 
Spray (APS) Technique”. The project focuses on developing indigenous fuel cell technology using lignite fly ash-derived 
materials. The study aims to create efficient and cost-effective 
energy conversion systems. The project is ongoing, with material preparation and preliminary research activities 
in progress.
11.  Microbial Technologies for Crop Cultivation under 
Agri-voltaic Systems
  An R&D project has been undertaken by CARD, NLCIL 
with Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Coimbatore on 
“Microbial technologies for Crop Cultivation under Shade – Agri-voltaic system”. The project focuses on studying crop 
growth and microbial interactions under solar-integrated 
agricultural systems. The study aims to enhance productivity 
and resource utilisation.
  The project is ongoing, with crop cultivation activities 
initiated and growth monitoring underway.
12.  UV-Assisted Self-Cleaning Ceramic Membrane 
System for Water Recycling
  CARD, NLCIL is collaborating with National Institute of 
Technology, Rourkela (NITR) on “Design and Development 
of UV-Assisted Self-Cleaning Filters Using Ceramic 
Membranes for Recycling Circulating Water Blowdown from 
Thermal Power Stations”. The project focuses on developing 
advanced filtration systems for treatment and reuse of 
industrial wastewater. The study aims to improve efficiency 
and support zero liquid discharge practices. The project is 
ongoing, with system design completed and laboratory-scale 
development in progress.
13. Drone-Based AI/ML System for Boiler Inspection
  A collaborative R&D project has been undertaken by CARD, 
NLCIL with Indian Institute of Technology, Hyderabad (IITH) on “Enhancing Boiler Inspection in Coal/Lignite 
Based Power Plant Using Drone with AI/ML and Thermal 
Imaging”. The project focuses on developing intelligent drone 
systems with thermal imaging and artificial intelligence for 
inspection of power plant boilers. The study aims to improve 
safety and enable predictive maintenance. The project is 
ongoing, with system design finalised and testing activities 
in progress.
14.  AI-Based Autonomous Lignite Dust Collection 
System
  CARD, NLCIL has taken up a collaborative R&D project 
with Indian Institute of Information Technology, Design and 
Manufacturing (IIITDM), Kancheepuram on “AI and vision integrated autonomous mobile lignite dust collection system 
for cleaning bunker floors”. The project focuses on developing 
an autonomous robotic system for safe and efficient removal of lignite dust. The study aims to reduce manual intervention 
and improve workplace safety. The project is ongoing, with 
system design and development activities under progress.
15.  Renewable Hydrogen Production from Biogas 
using Solar Heating
  A joint R&D initiative has been undertaken by CARD, NLCIL 
with Annamalai University, Chidambaram on “An innovative 
method for generating renewable hydrogen from biogas using 
advanced parabolic solar heating”. The project focuses on 
developing hydrogen production using solar-driven methane 
cracking from biogas. The study aims to utilise renewable 
energy for clean fuel generation. The project is ongoing, 
with process evaluation and system development activities 
in progress.16.  Automated Conveyor Belt Monitoring and Defect Detection System
  CARD, NLCIL has undertaken a collaborative R&D project 
with Annamalai University, Chidambaram on “Automated 
Monitoring and Defect Detection System for Conveyor 
Belts in Mining Operations: Increasing Reliability and 
Efficiency through Real Time Data Interpretation and Rapid 
Response Alerts”. The project focuses on developing real-
time monitoring systems using sensors and intelligent data 
processing for early defect detection. The study aims to enhance safety and operational reliability. The project is 
ongoing, with initial system development and implementation 
activities under progress.

Annexure – III
Management Discussion
and Analysis
India Economy
India’s economy exhibited exceptional resilience in FY 2025-26, 
successfully navigating global market conditions through steady 
domestic fundamentals. According to the National Statistical 
Office (NSO), India’s real GDP grew by a robust 7.7% during the 
year, underpinned by strong private consumption, vibrant services 
expansion and sustained public capital spending. 
Over the past four years, average retail inflation, as measured by 
the Consumer Price Index (CPI), has followed a clear downward 
trajectory, declining steadily from 6.7% in FY 2022-23 to 1.7% in 2025-26. To further nurture growth and support long-term investment momentum alongside easing price pressures, the 
Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) 
maintained a calibrated easing framework, establishing the policy 
repo rate at 5.25% following progressive rate adjustments. This 
monetary flexibility was anchored by benign core inflation, which 
remained comfortably contained around 3.6%, even as input cost 
dynamics in key industrial sectors like metals and energy remained 
closely monitored.
[Source: PIB, Economic Survey 2025-26]Outlook
Looking ahead to FY 2026-27, economic growth is expected to remain steady at 6.6%, supported by a revival in urban consumption, aided by direct tax rationalisation, and resilient 
rural demand, driven by strong agricultural momentum following 
proactive climate-mitigation measures. Balanced input costs are 
expected to support corporate margins and fiscal stability, while 
improved real wages and stabilising core inflation will further lift discretionary spending, a key metric for the auto and retail sectors. 
The RBI is maintaining a data-dependent, neutral stance, using 
calibrated liquidity management to ensure price dynamics remain within target while supporting sustainable credit flows. Crucially, 
robust momentum across core infrastructure sectors, driven by 
surging electricity demand and expansion in mining, will reinforce 
high-capacity utilisation and private capital expenditure, fueling 
sustained long-term industrial momentum.
While international market shifts call for strategic adaptability, 
India’s domestic growth trajectory remains securely anchored. 
Despite global energy price pressures and supply chain headwind 
stemming from the West Asia conflict, headline CPI inflation is 
projected to pick up from a low base of 2.1% in FY 2025-26 to 
a manageable 5.1% in FY 2026-27, with core inflation remaining 
well-contained. Quarterly CPI is expected to follow a stable trajectory: 4.2% in Q1, 5.1% in Q2, 5.9% in Q3, and 5.4% in Q4, with inflation risks viewed as broadly balanced. Real GDP 
expansion across quarters, 6.6% in Q1, 6.3% in Q2, 6.5% in Q3, 
and 6.8% in Q4, reflects a resilient domestic foundation for durable economic progress.Global Economy
Demonstrating strong fundamental resilience, the global 
economy maintained steady progress throughout CY25 across 
diverse regional markets and sectors. Worldwide economic 
output expanded by 3.5%, sustained by underlying momentum 
as markets successfully adapted to higher interest rates, normalising inflation, and shifting geopolitical dynamics. Advanced economies achieved a stable, sustainable growth 
pace of 1.9% while balancing tighter monetary frameworks and 
changing trade flows. However, trade policy uncertainties and 
potential cost pressures stemming from U.S. tariff impositions 
continue to cast a shadow over near-term global investment and market stability. Meanwhile, emerging and developing economies continued to serve as powerful growth engines, 
expanding by 4.5% on the back of vibrant domestic consumption 
and strategic public investments. 
Global price pressures eased noticeably. Headline inflation 
moderated to 4.1%, supported by proactive monetary policies 
and stable energy costs during the year. While service sector 
inflation and policy shifts called for prudent capital allocation, 
businesses and investors navigated the year with strategic focus and measured confidence.Outlook
According to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) World 
Economic Outlook, July 2026, global growth is projected 
to moderate to 3.0% in CY26, before rising to 3.4% in CY27. 
Renewed geopolitical disruptions, driven largely by the West 
Asia war are pushing energy prices upwards and disrupting 
global trade flow, resulting in global inflation to increase to an 
estimated 4.7% in CY26. However, positive tailwinds include 
accelerated AI technology investment, ongoing real wage 
recovery, and accommodative monetary policy frameworks. 
Growth in advanced economies is projected at 1.7% in CY26

Global Energy Sector
In CY25, the global energy sector demonstrated steady expansion, 
with global energy demand growing by approximately 1.3%, 
aligning with the decade average according to the Global Energy 
Review by the International Energy Agency (IEA). Demand was led by the power sector as global electricity consumption 
grew by nearly 3.0%, well above overall energy demand growth. 
Geographically, emerging and developing economies continued to drive over three-quarters of global energy demand growth. China 
remained the largest single contributor, while India maintained strong energy consumption momentum supported by robust industrial expansion. In advanced economies, energy demand stayed stable, with the US recording a 2.3% electricity demand 
increase driven by manufacturing and data centres, while European 
demand stabilised.
In the global energy supply mix in CY25, Solar PV became the single largest contributor to demand growth at over 25%, the 
first time a renewable source led global primary energy growth, 
followed by Natural Gas at 17%. Together, renewables and nuclear met nearly 60% of all new energy demand.Natural Gas demand grew at a measured pace of around 1.2% to 
reach new highs, supported by steady industrial consumption in 
North America, Europe, and Asia, where gas continued to support power reliability alongside variable clean energy sources.
Global coal demand rose by 0.4% in 2025. China’s demand remained flat as renewables offset industrial shifts. Strong monsoons reduced India’s coal power generation. In contrast, 
US coal usage jumped 10%, driven by gas-to-coal switching and 
surging electricity demand.
Oil demand growth moderated to 0.7% in CY25, with its overall 
share in the energy mix continuing to adjust. Rapid electric vehicle 
adoption, with global annual sales exceeding 20 million units, 
constrained road fuel demand, though increases in aviation and 
petrochemical feedstocks provided offset.
Electricity demand was pronounced across emerging markets, led by China and Southeast Asia. In advanced economies, power consumption was driven by building cooling, industrial 
electrification, and digital infrastructure. Accelerated AI and data India’s Energy Sector
India continued to anchor global energy demand expansion in 2025, recording the world's second-highest absolute increase in energy usage, a growth trajectory that surpassed the combined 
demand additions of all advanced nations. Strong macroeconomic 
momentum, accelerating industrialisation, and rising per capita

As per the Energy Statistics India 2026 publication by the Ministry

manufacturing, transport, residential usage, and agriculture. 
Fossil fuels retain the primary share in India’s energy matrix, with 
coal leading at 59% of total supply, followed by crude oil at 30%,

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), emerging 
and developing economies will account for nearly 80% of net 
global power demand expansion through 2030, with India serving 
as a primary anchor of this growth. As the world’s fastest-growing 
major economy, India is projected to lead global energy demand 
expansion, fuelled by sustained industrial development, rapid 
urbanisation, and broad-based economic momentum.

of energy, cementing its role as a key engine of the global energy

Tax Write-Off & Accelerated Depreciation Rules 
for Rooftop Solar
Under the self-owned CAPEX model, businesses can claim a 
40% Accelerated Depreciation tax deduction under Section 
32 in Year 1, significantly lowering taxable income compared 
to the standard 15% rate. Entities under the Old Tax Regime 
can add a 20% initial depreciation under Section 32(1)(iia) 
for a 60% total first-year write-off (unavailable under the 
115BAA/115BAB concessional tax regimes). To get the full 
Year 1 deduction, the plant must be commissioned before 
October 3 ( 180 days of use). If commissioned after October 
3 (<180 days), the allowable first-year claim is halved to 20% 
under concessional regimes or 30% under the old regime. 
These write-offs require direct ownership, excluding 
third-party OPEX/RESCO PPAs, and allow capitalising 
uncredited GST into the asset base.
Solar Power
Solar power leads India's shift toward clean energy. From just 
2.82 GW in FY 2014–15, total solar capacity expanded 53.28x to 
reach 150.26 GW in FY 2025-26. A historic single-year addition 
of 29.70 GW during the year under review highlights this surging 
momentum. Today, solar forms the bedrock of the country's 
renewable energy basket, reinforced by expanding decentralised 
rooftop systems and a maturing local supply chain. Targeted policy 
mechanisms, ranging from dedicated solar park infrastructure to 
enhanced grid connectivity and local module manufacturing under 
the Make in India initiative, continue to drive this unprecedented 
scale-up.

Short-term Power Market in India
India’s short-term power market, underpinned by evolving Deviation Settlement Mechanism (DSM) regulations, plays a critical role in satisfying the nation's dynamic energy demand. By granting operational agility to both buyers and sellers, it 
strengthens market efficiency, improves forecasting compliance, 
and enables real-time grid balancing as demand and generation 
profiles fluctuate.
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission data indicates that short-term trading comprised 17.7% of nationwide power generation during FY 2025-26, with long-term agreements and 
intra-state arrangements making up the remaining 82.3%. These 
figures highlight how short-term transactions deliver the necessary 
liquidity and market responsiveness to stabilise the grid.
Key Features of CERC’s 2026 Second 
Amendment Regulations on Power Markets and Tariff Structures
• Designation of Grid-India as MCO: The CERC (Power 
Market) 2nd Amendment officially designates the Grid 
Controller of India Limited (Grid-India) as the single 
Market Coupling Operator (MCO). Grid-India oversees 
centralised price discovery and uniform market clearing 
across both the Day-Ahead (DAM) and Real-Time 
(RTM) electricity markets. 
• Unified Market-Clearing Price (UMCP): Instead of individual power exchanges independently calculating local clearing prices, power exchanges submit anonymised, standardised bid data directly to the MCO. The MCO runs a centralised algorithm to 
compute a single, uniform market-clearing price across 
all platforms. 
• Tariff Integration for Energy Storage Systems (ESS): 
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) co-located with 
generation or transmission assets are integrated into a 
multi-part billing structure. This splits remuneration 
into Fixed Capacity Charges (for availability) and Energy 
Charges (for actual charge/discharge usage). 
• Normative Storage Performance Standards: The 2nd 
Amendment Tariff framework sets explicit performance 
baselines for storage projects, requiring a minimum 90% 
availability benchmark to claim full capacity charges 
and an 85% Round-Trip Efficiency (RTE) target, along 
with structured financial incentives for operational 
efficiency gains.Growth in Power Generation (BU) (Over the Years)

Source: CERC, (-) Export, (+) ImportRenewable Energy Certificates (RECs)
A total of 187.20 Lakh Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) were 
traded across power exchanges and bilateral licensee channels 
during FY 2025-26, representing a 5% year-over-year rise from the 178.29 Lakh RECs cleared in FY 2024-25.
Under the framework established by the CERC REC Regulations 
2022, the former division between solar and non-solar certificates 
was phased out in favour of a single, unified REC instrument. To 
incentivise emerging and capital-intensive clean technologies, this mechanism incorporates certificate multipliers, boosting 
both market appeal and financial feasibility for a broader range of 
renewable power projects.In Terms of Market Performance:
• The market clearing volume of RECs traded on power exchanges 
surged to 304.18 Lakh in FY 2024-25 
• The weighted average market clearing price of these RECs 
further declined to ₹225/MWh in FY 2024-25
